summary: This standards-track document describes how to build multilevel TRILL using IS-IS multilevel features with the unique nickname approach. Depending on how nicknames are managed, there are two main alternatives; this specifies one of them.

plainLanguage.summary: A big city is split into neighborhoods and every house keeps its own unique name. This explains that approach for TRILL.

questions: how do unique nicknames work in trill multilevel
what is unique nickname trill multilevel
how do trill border rbridges announce nicknames
subtitle: How a big TRILL campus is split into areas while every switch keeps one globally unique nickname.

tldr.problem: A single flat TRILL campus does not scale well, but splitting it into levels raises the question of how switch nicknames and multi-destination trees should work across areas.
tldr.mechanism: Using IS-IS multilevel, border RBridges announce which nicknames belong to which area, so every nickname stays unique across the whole campus and packets cross areas without any nickname rewriting. A new NickBlockFlags APPsub-TLV carries those announcements.
tldr.outcome: Border RBridges can be simpler than in the aggregated nickname approach, at the cost of less scalability for very large campuses.

today: RFC 8397 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted or updated. It specifies the unique nickname alternative; the aggregated nickname alternative is discussed in RFC 8243.

sections.title: Two Ways to Do Multilevel TRILL
sections.content:
The multiple-level feature of IS-IS can increase the scalability of TRILL, as discussed in RFC 8243. Making it work needs extensions for two things: how switch nicknames are managed and how distribution trees are handled.

There are two primary alternatives. The aggregated nickname approach gives nicknames to areas and lets border switches rewrite nickname fields as packets enter or leave an area. The unique nickname approach, which this document specifies, gives unique nicknames to all TRILL switches in the multilevel campus. Border RBridges advertise into a Level 1 area which nicknames are not available there, and advertise into Level 2 which nicknames the Level 1 area uses, so other areas cannot reuse them.

Because nicknames are globally valid, border RBridges do not rewrite the nickname field of TRILL data packets moving between Level 1 and Level 2. A border RBridge acting as a transit node also does not learn MAC addresses from those packets, and testing and maintenance operations across areas are simplified. The RFC says this might give simpler border RBridges, but the approach is less scalable and may be less well suited to very large campuses.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two ways to run a big city of switches. In one, each neighborhood reuses names and mail carriers relabel letters at the border. In this one, every house has a name nobody else uses, so no relabeling is needed.

sections.title: Unicast Routing Across Areas
sections.content:
The RFC walks through an example where source S in Area X sends a frame to destination D in Area Y. RB27 is the ingress RBridge in Area X, RB2 and RB3 are border RBridges, and RB44 is next to D. RB27 has learned that D is connected to nickname 44, and RB2 has learned that nickname 44 is reachable through RB3.

RB27 encapsulates the Ethernet frame in a TRILL header with ingress nickname 27 and egress nickname 44. RB2 has announced in the Level 1 IS-IS instance in Area X that it owns all nicknames of other areas, including 44, so the packet is routed to RB2. It then crosses Level 2 to RB3, which advertised in Level 2 that it owns nickname 44. RB3 forwards into Area Y without changing the ingress nickname 27 or the egress nickname 44. When RB44 decapsulates the packet, it learns that S is attached to nickname 27.

Each switch calculates only its own piece of the path: RB27 the segment in Area X, RB2 the segment in Level 2, and RB3 the segment from itself to RB44.
sections.plainLanguage: A letter leaves with the sender's and receiver's house names on it. The first border post says "I can get that to the other neighborhood," the next one takes it the last stretch, and the names on the envelope never change.

sections.title: Local and Global Distribution Trees
sections.content:
Multi-destination traffic is flooded along distribution trees. The scope of a tree is set by its root nickname: a tree with a Level 2 root nickname is global, and a tree with a Level 1 root nickname is local. Border RBridges announce global trees only for Data Labels (VLAN or FGL) that span areas, using APPsub-TLVs from RFC 7968. Based on the Data Label, an ingress RBridge decides whether a global or local tree is used.

A local tree spans only its own area, and behaves as in RFC 6325 otherwise. A multi-destination packet whose egress nickname is the root of a local tree MUST NOT be leaked into Level 2. For global trees, the RBridge with the highest tree root priority in Level 2 advertises the set of global trees, and a border RBridge with the highest root priority in each area advertises the global tree roots into that area. It MUST also advertise a set of local tree roots, and the two sets MUST NOT overlap because they have different flooding scopes.

When a multi-destination packet uses a global tree, it is flooded using the part of the tree in Area X, then the part in Level 2, then the part in Area Y. Legacy TRILL switches that do not understand the tree-selection APPsub-TLVs need configuration so that Data Labels used globally in Level 2 are disabled on them, and global trees MUST be pruned at border switches by Data Label.
sections.plainLanguage: Some announcements are only for one neighborhood and some are for the whole city. The type of loudspeaker, a local one or a city-wide one, decides how far the message goes.

sections.title: Allocating Nicknames Between Levels
sections.content:
Multilevel TRILL builds on IS-IS multilevel. Border RBridges sit in both a Level 1 area and Level 2, with independent adjacency state machines and independent link-state flooding for each level. That keeps Level 1 information inside the area and Level 2 information inside Level 2 unless something is deliberately leaked.

Level 2 RBridges contend for nicknames in the range 0xF000 through 0xFFBF as in RFC 6325, using Level 2 LSPs. The highest-priority border router for a Level 1 area contends in Level 2 for blocks of nicknames from 0x0001 to 0xEFFF. Blocks of 64 aligned on multiples of 64 are RECOMMENDED. The outcome of that contention decides which blocks are available to an area and which are used elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: Before moving in, each neighborhood has to claim blocks of house names so nobody else picks the same ones.

sections.title: The NickBlockFlags APPsub-TLV
sections.content:
A border RBridge MUST announce into its area the ownership of all external nicknames reachable through it, and MUST announce into Level 2 the ownership of all nicknames within its area. The ordinary Nickname Sub-TLV could do this, but it is uneconomic for a mass of nicknames, so border RBridges SHOULD use the new NickBlockFlags APPsub-TLV, type 24.

Its length is 2 + 4*K, where K is the number of nickname blocks. It has an OK bit and a reserved field (RESV, sent as zero and ignored on receipt), followed by the blocks, each a starting and an ending nickname.

  • With OK set to 1, the blocks belong to the border RBridge's attached Level 1 area. The TLV is advertised in both Level 1 and Level 2, and Level 2 RBridges route to the originating border RBridge as if it owned those nicknames.
  • With OK set to 0, the blocks are in use in Level 2 or other areas and are not available in this area. The TLV is advertised into Level 1 only. TRILL Data packets whose egress nickname is neither in these ranges nor announced by any RBridge in the area MUST be discarded.

Multiple border RBridges may serve the same area, and each may advertise a subset of the nickname space for load balancing; optimizing that is outside the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of listing every house name one by one, the border post posts a sign saying "names from here to there are taken." One extra mark on the sign says whether they belong to this neighborhood or to somewhere else.

sections.title: Capability Indication and Mixed Areas
sections.content:
All border RBridges MUST understand the NickBlockFlags APPsub-TLV, and non-border RBridges in an area should. An RBridge that understands it MUST say so in its TRILL-VER Sub-TLV. If some RBridges in an area do not understand it, the border RBridges MUST also use the traditional Nickname Sub-TLV to announce the nicknames in blocks whose OK bit is 0, and the available nickname range should be configured on those traditional RBridges.

Unique nickname areas can be mixed with aggregated nickname areas. Nickname usage MUST be planned so that nicknames used in a unique nickname area or in Level 2 are never used in any other area. Reuse is allowed only among aggregated nickname areas. Border RBridges of an aggregated area MUST announce nicknames heard from Level 2 into their area, but do not announce their area's nicknames into Level 2. Each such border RBridge appears on the global tree as a single node.
sections.plainLanguage: Old and new switches can live together as long as the old ones are told by hand which names are free. And neighborhoods that reuse names must stay separate from neighborhoods whose names are unique.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because multilevel TRILL uses IS-IS multilevel facilities, flooding of link-state information is confined to a Level 1 area or to Level 2, which also confines the effects of malicious events. But unique nickname areas share one nickname space, so border RBridges must leak nickname information between levels, and nickname-related events in one area can affect others.

A malicious device could fake the NickBlockFlags APPsub-TLV to claim a range of nicknames and attract packets meant for other RBridges. RBridges SHOULD therefore be configured to use the IS-IS Authentication TLV (10), especially in PDUs carrying the NickBlockFlags APPsub-TLV, so forged PDUs can be authenticated and discarded using RFC 5310.

If border RBridges do not prune multi-destination tree traffic for Data Labels configured as area-local, traffic could be delivered to end stations in that Data Label in other areas, violating constraints that require delivery within a single area. For general TRILL security considerations, see RFC 6325.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could post a fake sign claiming a block of names and steal other people's mail. The fix is to sign the signs so fakes get thrown out.
